HEADLINE: After 45 years, Wheeler drives back to London
TEXT:
Travel The Lonely Planet co-founder is retracing his steps.

Forty-five years after his life-defining overland journey from London to Sydney on the Hippie Trail, Lonely Planet co-founder Tony Wheeler is doing it all again, in reverse.

But rather than slumming it in a £65 Mini (later offloaded for £70 in Kabul) as he and wife Maureen did in 1972, this time Wheeler is driving an MGB he bought and spent "an absolute fortune" on especially for the trip.

The car, a 1973 MGB GT hard top, was made the same year the Wheelers published their first Lonely Planet guide - Across Asia on the Cheap - and Wheeler says "there is a nice sort of symmetry in going back and doing it all again".

The 1972 trip took nine months and famously ended with Wheeler and his new wife Maureen down to their last 27 cents. It also led to the founding of Lonely Planet, now the world's largest guidebook publisher, which the Wheelers and partner John Singleton would eventually sell to the BBC for almost $270 million.

On that trip, Wheeler and Maureen regularly skipped lunch, slept rough and ran out of fuel as they meandered across Asia.

This time pretty much everything is different. For starters, Pakistan and Afghanistan are off limits, so this tour that started in Bangkok in early April is going via China and the "Stans" of Central Asia before returning to more familiar territory in Iran. More consequential for the travelling itself is that driving across the Silk Road in a convoy of eight MGBs, with seven retired or partly retired MG enthusiast couples from Sydney and Melbourne, requires infinitely more planning.

"Forty-five years ago each day we just made up what was going to happen the next day," Wheeler says this week from China, where the group is a third of the way into the three-month trip. "We thought we'll aim for there and when we got there we had no idea what was going to happen.

"Whereas this trip, everything is organised. We know where we're staying every night until early July, which is unusual."

Another major difference is that this time there will be no Maureen. Wheeler says his wife and Lonely Planet co-founder had planned to join him for the leg across Iran and Turkey, but other commitments had forced her to pull out. Instead their daughter, Tashi, will join him for that leg.

As for the ageing cars, all built in 1973 or earlier, Wheeler says so far there have only been a couple of minor problems but nothing that has caused any serious delays.

Wheeler, 70, says the pace of change in rural China has been amazing.

"I can't get over the amount of stuff they are building. You see it in the cities, but out in the country it's being built everywhere.

"It's been mountainous ever since we crossed in from Laos and the freeways just cross valleys and run through the hills. The cost must be phenomenal."

"Every city we've been in has two or three brand new bridges. And they're big bridges, they're not little at all. It's like building the Sydney Harbour Bridge once a week all over the country."

Wheeler sees the huge numbers of Chinese travelling both locally and internationally as an even more significant driver of change than the internet or budget airlines. He says the way young Chinese are embracing independent travel, and their willingness to use Lonely Planet books to do it, is portentous.

"My view is that in the end the Chinese will buy [Lonely Planet]. I can see that happening one day ... There is that Lonely Planet fascination there."

The publisher is currently owned by reclusive American tobacco billionaire Brad Kelley, who bought if from the BBC in 2013.

HEADLINE: Police admit illegally getting phone records
TEXT:
Australian Federal Police commissioner Andrew Colvin said Australians should still have full confidence in the nation's new metadata laws even though one of his investigators illegally accessed the telephone records of a journalist who received a leak of sensitive information.

Attorney-General George Brandis argued the contentious metadata laws were a necessary national security measure when they were introduced 18 months ago.

But the Federal Police was forced to admit, late Friday, it had improperly accessed the metadata of a journalist earlier this year - without first obtaining a warrant - in the course of investigating a leak.

The AFP has not informed the journalist his or her telephone records had been improperly accessed and Mr Colvin did not guarantee the journalist would ever be told once the investigation was completed.

"Once the investigation has finished, we will have to consider that," Mr Colvin said.

Media Entertainment Arts Alliance chief Paul Murphy said despite all the requirements put in place before journalists' information could be accessed, the system still failed.

"This is an attack on press freedom," he said.

Although Mr Colvin said the AFP had destroyed the information obtained and "self-reported" to the Commonwealth Ombudsman two days ago, the AFP will still be audited by the Ombudsman in an independent investigation starting next Friday.

HEADLINE: Energy projects pipeline gains support
TEXT:
The federal government should establish a pipeline of energy projects that can be rigorously assessed as it prepares to take on billions of dollars of debt to boost infrastructure investment, experts say.

Infrastructure Australia's priority list is skewed towards transport and water projects, and does not include energy projects.

Given the public discussion and "angst" over electricity blackouts, gas shortages and rising energy costs, energy projects should be added to IA's list, said Bruce Tanner, chief operating officer of engineering group Arup. "In a lot of cases that will be about storage."

The government has started looking for solutions to the energy crisis, committing to a $2 billion expansion of Snowy Hydro and investigating the potential to build a gas pipeline connecting the North-West Shelf with the eastern states.

John Clarke, founding director of the Infrastructure Capital Group, said the prohibition on unconventional gas exploration in NSW and Victoria was contributing to gas shortages. "Rather than a 'knee-jerk', politically-based prohibition, there needs to be a clear set of exploration principles developed, and a sensible assessment against these on a case-by-case basis," Mr Clarke said.

IA chief executive Philip Davies said the group, an independent statutory body, would review any projects over $100 million.

IA would also review any investments by the Northern Australia Infrastructure Fund over $100 million, he said. India's Adani Group wants to borrow $1 billion from the fund to help pay for rail links from the coast to its proposed $22 billion Carmichael coal mine in Queensland.

John Matthews, a partner at EY specialising in infrastructure, said the Commonwealth's plans to distinguish between "good" and "bad" debt in the budget - with borrowing for economically beneficial infrastructure considered "good" - made sense.

"A lot of our public debate has been either demonising debt or putting an undue focus on the surplus or the deficit and we've been missing opportunities to invest in things that would develop the country."

Some infrastructure specialists have raised concerns about the government's plans to spend $10 billion on an inland rail line between Brisbane and Melbourne, saying the amount of freight travelling between states may have declined since the project was first mooted as more goods are being imported from overseas.

Mr Clarke said the government's proposed infrastructure financing unit was unnecessary intervention and it should instead directly subsidise projects.

"There is extensive debt and equity funding from the private sector, both from domestic and international institutions, for all 'sensible' infrastructure development projects in Australia," he said. "If such projects are not 'sensible' and the private sector turns them down, then the government should either provide an explicit subsidy for them or dismiss the project and move on."

ECOM director James Rosenwax said the government needed to look beyond financial returns on single road, rail or transport projects and consider the broader social impact infrastructure investment could provide, such as adding bike and walking paths to encourage people to exercise.

HEADLINE: ACTIVE OR PASSIVE?
TEXT: In Australia last year 700 actively managed funds couldn't match the ASX index and investors are turning in droves to passively managed index trackers. Is it time to join the rush?

HEADLINE: AAA alert: inland rail project may not pass the 'good debt' test
TEXT:
A deal between Nationals leader Barnaby Joyce and Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull is behind the government's plan to rack up at least $1 billion in "good debt" building an inland railway that experts say will bring marginal economic benefit and could threaten the AAA credit rating.

Any surge in government borrowing with so-called "good debt" could weaken Australia's hold on its AAA credit rating because ratings agencies worry more about the nation's ability to service a ballooning debt pile than the quality of assets underpinning it.

The message from both Moody's Investors Service and S&P Global appears at odds with assurances given this week by Treasurer Scott Morrison that the agencies would not be spooked by the accrual of so-called good debt in order to build assets which generated income and enhanced productivity. Because the government would own the assets, there would be no impact on the budget bottom line and, hence, the planned return to surplus.

Their judgment is ultimately dependent on the overall government debt burden as well as its capacity to pay interest costs, according to the agency's policy documents and a statement to AFR Weekend.

AFR Weekend can reveal that Mr Joyce secured Mr Turnbull's support for the rail link - which has been touted for two decades - after threatening to withdraw support for the airport. Sources said the Nationals had misgivings about Badgerys Creek because they believe regional flights will take off and land there, disadvantaging their constituents because they would then face long taxi or train rides into the CBD.

The Nationals' preference was to lift the curfew at Sydney's existing airport to enable regional flights to continue landing there. In return for surrendering this demand, Mr Joyce negotiated support for the rail link. The government will part-fund the $10 billion project with the private sector.

Garry Bowditch, executive director of the University of Sydney's Better Infrastructure Initiative, said the government needed to spend more time analysing the forecast benefits of projects and how it could better use existing infrastructure before taking on debt to build new projects.

"Mega projects have been slow to deliver higher productivity and tangible results for the economy," Mr Bowditch said. "Just because the government says we should build a railway doesn't mean that is the best solution to a problem."

Some infrastructure specialists have raised concerns about the government's plans to spend $10 billion on an inland rail line between Brisbane and Melbourne, pointing out that the amount of freight travelling between states may have declined since the project was first mooted as more goods are imported from overseas.

Inland Rail is not one of Infrastructure Australia's seven "high priority" projects, which include Sydney's WestConnex motorway and Western Sydney Airport and Melbourne's new metro system. It has an estimated cost benefit ratio of 1.1, meaning benefits exceed costs only slightly. The railway is, however, considered one of 11 "priority projects" with upgrades of the east coast's Pacific Motorway and the Hobart science and technology precinct.

IA has warned that a fall in demand for Australia's coal exports, weak oil prices, reduced demand for interstate freight, and upgrades to NSW's Newell Highway could hurt the economic case for Inland Rail.

Australian Industry Group chief executive Innes Willox welcomed the strategy but urged the government to rely on Infrastructure Australia to assess projects to avoid bad investments.

"An important consideration is the risk of making it too easy for governments to approve investments in projects that do not stack up to careful scrutiny," he said.

"One way to manage this risk would be to insist that only debt used to finance the most rigorously and transparently evaluated investments could qualify as 'good debt'. There could, for instance, be a requirement that 'good debt' status could be achieved after a positive evaluation of a project by an open and independent agency such as Infrastructure Australia. Such a constraint would inhibit the emergence of debt-fuelled pork-barreling."

Mr Morrison announced that debt would be differentiated between good and bad debt in part to pave the way for a large infrastructure spend while not jeopardising the path to surplus nor threatening the AAA rating. Two projects the government is likely to fund in full or in part are the second Sydney airport at Badgerys Creek, and an inland rail link from Melbourne to Brisbane.

S&P refused to comment ahead of the May 9 budget on Mr Morrison's plans to overhaul the way the government accounts for debt.

However, the agency's ratings methodology clearly indicates its analysts are bound to emphasise the quantity, rather than quality, of Australia's debt.

Furthermore S&P warns in its documentation that it is particularly attuned to attempts by governments to shift debt "off budget" to flatter headline deficit numbers.

For that reason, the agency states in its key ratings policy document that changes in the "general government debt stock" as a percentage of GDP is a better indicator of "fiscal performance" than the reported deficit.

"In addition, the headline deficit is sometimes affected by political and other considerations, possibly creating strong incentives to move expenditures off budget," S&P says in its formal global sovereign rating methodology, which was last updated in late 2014.

The policy document underscores how Mr Morrison's scope to ramp up borrowing for infrastructure remains heavily constrained by the need to retain the AAA rating.

A credit rating downgrade would not only deliver a major blow to the Coalition's claim to superior economic management, it could also drive up the cost to taxpayers of servicing the nation's burgeoning debt burden, which is forecast to peak in 2019-20 at 30.6 per cent of gross domestic product - or $604 billion.

Moody's said yesterday that indicated it may be prepared to give the Treasurer some wriggle-room to borrow for infrastructure - but only if the spending generates a strong economic return that strengthens the Commonwealth's ability to pay back the debt.

Moody's associate managing director Marie Diron also warned that the economic quality of infrastructure spending can be difficult to measure.

"When the investment occurs, there is uncertainty about the degree to which it will effectively boost growth," she said.

"In our assessment, we consider the nature of government spending and the likelihood that it will support growth over the medium term."

She pointed out that the overall level of debt is the key.

"In the case of Australia, its general government debt burden is just under 40 per cent of GDP, in line with the median level of AAA-rated sovereigns."

HEADLINE: ResMed says 'connected care' drives sales
TEXT:
ResMed chief executive Mick Farrell says investment in cloud computing technology that helps patients be more engaged with their health is driving solid growth in the medical device maker's core business.

More than 3 million ResMed ventilation machines that are connected to the cloud are used by sufferers of sleep apnoea.

Such "connected care" allows patients to better monitor their health, and with smartphone apps such as ResMed's MyAir, has helped to improve adherence to treatment schedules from 60 per cent to 80 per cent in the past three to four years, Mr Farrell said.

"We encourage them to stick with their therapy and as part of that they buy more masks," he said.

Sales of masks and machines, which stem from ResMed's origins in the late '80s as an Australian start-up, rose 6 per cent to $US479.2 million ($641.7 million) in the quarter ended March 31. The rate of growth was 7 per cent when currency effects were excluded.

However, when ResMed's health software business Brightree, which was acquired in April 2016, was included in the numbers revenue growth surged 13 per cent to $US514.2 million. Brightree provides software to care organisations that help with services such as document, inventory and medicine management.

Third-quarter net profit for the dual-listed company rose 3 per cent to $US107.4 million.

Wilsons analyst Shane Storey said ResMed's revenue came in 2 per cent lower than the consensus forecasts among analysts but earnings per share of US71¢ (up 3 per cent) was in line with expectations. Dr Storey highlighted market share growth from sales of ResMed's AirSense10 machine.

ResMed shares listed on the ASX fell 4.0 per cent to $9.16 on Friday after hitting a 12-month high of $9.54 the day prior. The stock has still gained 22 per cent in the past year.

HEADLINE: Bezos isn't focused on Australia - yet
TEXT:
Amazon's quarterly earnings release on Friday morning may provide the tiniest glimmer of hope for Australian retailers.

It hinted, ever so slightly, that for all the excitement and fear about the e-commerce titan's imminent arrival, its global expansion focus at the moment lies not on these shores, but elsewhere.

In the earnings release provided to investors there were 10 references to India (a gigantic market that is critical for the company, and where it is waging a fierce battle with local VC-backed player Flipkart). The UK was mentioned four times, Japan and Germany warranted three mentions, Mexico got one, even Sweden, where it is building a distribution centre, received a shout-out.

Australia, the world's 12th biggest economy where Amazon finally confirmed plans to bring its full e-commerce service: nothing. In fact, the only thing remotely Australian in the release was a mention for the actress Cate Blanchett, who made a film that is using Amazon's new digital film distribution service.

There was no mention of Australia on the ensuing earnings call either, according to a transcript provided by S&P Capital IQ (India got another 11, Mexico and the UK one each).

OK, we are probably clutching at straws here. Perhaps it's not surprising Amazon is so heavily focused on India, which has the world's second biggest population, and where it has invested billions, and not really thinking about a rich but small market where its presence is still minimal.

In any case, the rest of the result should keep Australian retail executives nervous.

Amazon maintained its two-decade-long streak of double-digital sales growth, posting revenue of $US35.7 billion ($47.8 billion), up 23 per cent from a year earlier. For the sixth straight quarter, the historically profit averse company turned a profit, booking net income of $US724 million, up 41 per cent from a year ago.

Over the past 12 months it generated $US10.2 billion in free cash flow (that being the metric chief executive Jeff Bezos really cares about) up from $US6.7 billion for the same period last year. It forecast another quarter of double-digit sales growth ahead, and in after-hours trading shares in the company were up by about 4 per cent.

Tellingly, Amazon international operations were a drag on the results. International net sales grew 16 per cent to $US21 billion, but the company booked an operating loss of $US481 million, a near four times widening from a year ago.

Australian retailers should definitely not take comfort from that. Much of the deeper loss would have come from India, but it still shows Amazon has the will, and resources, to sacrifice short-term margins and profits for long-term dominance.

"It's still Day 1 for e-commerce in India, and I assure you that we'll keep investing in technology and infrastructure [in the country]," CEO Bezos said in the release. Amazon tends not to do things in half measures, and if it applies that level of focus to Australia, then watch out.

HEADLINE: Atlassian growth wards off threat from big rivals
TEXT:
Australian technology export Atlassian has laid out plans for continued strong revenue growth as its growing suite of products protects it from the threat of an ambush by big-name rivals like Slack and Microsoft.

In its quarterly earnings call Friday morning, Atlassian's leadership team, including co-founders Mike Cannon-Brookes, Scott Farquhar and long-time president Jay Simons, had a strong story to tell as revenue and customer numbers all moved healthily in the right direction, with a positive debut on the books for its $US425 million ($577 million) January acquisition of Trello.

For the quarter Atlassian booked revenue of $US159.9 million, which was up 36 per cent from $US117.9 million this time last year, while analysts were particularly buoyed by a 68 per cent increase in free cash flow to $68.3 million, which Mr Farquhar observed was more free cash flow than the company produced in all of 2014-15 combined.

Overall Atlassian booked a net loss of $US17.5 million for the quarter, which compared to a loss of $US1.1 million last year, but this was largely attributed to increased equity payments aimed at incentivising and retaining staff, rather than a drop off in business performance.

Investors were more interested in the customer growth profile of the company as a whole, and would have liked statistics showing project management app Trello had brought with it 12,789 new customers for Atlassian.

The company overall grew its customer numbers by 26 per cent year on year to just over 85,000.

Mr Farquhar said the company had a long-term goal that incorporated potential clients across the "Fortune 500,000", but in the near term was well on course to crack the 100,000 barrier.

It also provided positive forward guidance for the full year, with total revenue expected to be in the range of $US616 million to $US618 million, and free cash flow expected to be $US173 million to $US177 million.

The numbers led to a positive reaction on the Nasdaq, with the stock up a modest 1.5 per cent in after-hours trading to close out the day up almost 2 per cent at $US33.47.

The company now has a market cap of $US7.5 billion ($10 billion), which would make it the 37th largest company on the ASX.

It is not without challenges on the horizon, however, with competitors like Slack for its HipChat messaging product and Microsoft's move to go all in on the same space with its Teams product late last year. Even Facebook has begun making a concerted push to make the switch from workplace productivity drain to improvement tool.

Mr Simons, however, was keen to tell analysts that the diversity of Atlassian's product stack - in addition to an increasingly vibrant marketplace fed by external application developers - meant the company is really not in a life-or-death battle with anyone.

Atlassian is competing on enough fronts, and in big enough markets, that headline threats from tech behemoths are less dramatic than they sound.

"We have been in this market for 15 years, so the competitive dynamics haven't really changed much in that time. Some of the names have changed," Mr Simons said.

"It is a big market that we are continuing to grow into, and I think one of our main advantages is the strength and breadth of the Team portfolio. We are building multiple products that fulfil really critical needs for teams ... so even in a situation where we are losing head to head against a particular competitor in a category, we still have an opportunity to sell around that competitor and we often do."

Mr Cannon-Brookes was also keen to stress to the market that Atlassian thrives alongside other technology companies, rather than needing to knock them off the map.

The company is increasingly transitioning customers to a cloud-based rather than on-premise server-based model, which is often defined by client organisations having a diaspora of tech suppliers.

HEADLINE: Platinum responds to profound changes
TEXT:
The decision by Kerr Neilson's Platinum Asset Management to slash fees on a range of international managed funds and launch several ASX-listed funds are in response to the powerful forces impacting Australian financial markets.

These forces are the heightened competition from low-cost, passive investment strategies, the increased power of the big four banks and AMP in distribution, and the international regulatory moves to make all aspects of investing more transparent.

Neilson, who is one of the country's most successful fund managers over the past 20 years, has cut his base fee from 1.5 per cent to 1.35 per cent and as low as 1.1 per cent when combined with a relative outperformance fee of 15 per cent.

These fee cuts will have a negative $24 million annualised impact on the revenue earned by Platinum's listed funds management company, which explains why the stock fell about 6.6 per cent on Friday to $4.66.

One analyst said Platinum would need to bring in about $3 billion in new funds under management to compensate for the fee cuts.

Platinum's fees have been cut in response to intense competition from passive investment funds, which charge fees between 15 basis points and 25 basis points.

To get an idea of the incredible economies of scale available in large passive asset management outfits you only need look at the latest numbers from global passive manager Vanguard. The average fee charged on its $US5.4 trillion in passive funds under management is 12 basis points.

But passive investment, which really means getting the index return, has not necessarily beaten active investment management over the long term.

When Neilson spoke to Chanticleer on Friday he pointed out that $1000 invested with him from the inception of his business 22 years ago would have increased in value by 13 times. An index fund would only be worth three times the initial investment.

Neilson says the single best bet over the past five to six years has been the US equity market and that has suited passive investment strategies.

He says the investment game may become more complicated if other markets around the world take the running. For example, he is bullish on Japan and Korea where the corporate sector is concentrating hard on distributing its free cash flow.

CLSA analyst Jan van der Schalk welcomed the changes at Platinum. "Platinum will have done their research and will have concluded that there's compensating FUM-flow upside to this change in fee structure," he said. "Furthermore, by introducing a performance fee element they're backing their investment process and talent.

"I have a sense that this is more about positioning Platinum for a future where you need to provide investors with as many access points into your business as possible, which is both smart and thoughtful."

The second important aspect of the Platinum announcement was the launch of two exchange traded managed funds later this year. These funds will allow investors to access Platinum's international and Asian equity strategies through the ASX.

These types of funds have already been launched by Magellan Financial Group.

This is a logical response to the tight grip that the big banks and AMP have on distribution through their control of 60 per cent of financial advisers and 90 per cent of investment platforms.

One leading financial adviser in Sydney said Platinum was signalling that unlisted managed funds would eventually be a thing of the past. The recent resurgence of interest in listed investment companies, including the launch of the Morphic Ethical Equities Fund, are further signs of the importance investors place on ASX liquidity.

One reason that LICs are attractive is because of the transparency about fees. They usually charge about 1 per cent of FUM. In other words, what you see is what you get.

An investor in a Platinum fund who was advised by a financial planner would have to pay an additional fee of about 1 per cent of FUM and a platform fee of about 50 basis points. All up the person would be paying more than 2 per cent even after the latest fee cuts are implemented in July.

The third powerful force impacting on the investment management industry is the regulatory reform coming into force in January next year called MIFID II. This reform, which is being driven by the European Securities and Markets Authority, will introduce new transparency, including the full disclosure of the costs and charges of investing. Brokerage costs for executing share trades will be disclosed separately to the cost of broker research.

There is general agreement this will force many analysts out of work or, at the very least, lead to the consolidation of research services.

Neilson says this reform will favour large investment management companies which will have the scale and financial strength to employ their own analysts.

It is possible that this last powerful market force will lead to further cuts in the fees charged to end investors, which can only be a good thing when it is increasingly difficult to earn double-digit returns.

Tatts rejects rival offer

The sudden fall in the share price of wagering and lotteries group Tatts Group on Friday would have provided a modicum of consolation to the losing bidder, the Pacific Consortium.

By the close of trading on Friday the market had clearly come to the view there will no longer be an auction for the target company and it will fall into the hands of Tabcorp.

Tatts shares fell about 3.8 per cent to $4.30 once the Pacific Consortium said it would walk away in response to the refusal of the Tatts board to grant due diligence.

The Pacific Consortium comprised four financial investors: First State Superannuation Scheme, Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Inc, as adviser to and manager of North Haven Infrastructure Partners II LP, one or more affiliates of Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co, and Macquarie Corporate Holdings.

The general view in the market is these financial investors would have broken up Tatts and probably sold its wagering business to Tabcorp.

It made it clear when it first approach Tatts in December that it really just wanted to get its hands on the lotteries business with its strong, predictable cash flows.

These sorts of business are perfect for carrying lots of debt in tax effective vehicles.

But the Tatts board, which is chaired by Harry Boon, came up with 10 reasons why it could not grant the Pacific Consortium due diligence.

The primary reason was that the share price was at $4.47. Of course that reason was significantly diluted by the sharemarket reaction.

There are some useful lessons to be taken away from this latest takeover battle.

First, a counter bidder keen on winning due diligence from a reluctant board needs to bid more than the bare minimum. Another 5¢c or 10¢ a share would have probably got the rival bidder over the line.

Second, shareholder pressure on boards will count for nothing if the directors think they risk breaching their fiduciary and legal obligations. Every sensible director will avoid opening themselves to litigation.

Third, uncertainty over regulatory decisions, including Australian Competition Tribunal decisions, can be ignored when it suits an incumbent board.

HEADLINE: Noske given jail time for insider deal
TEXT:
Former oil and gas executive Steven Noske will spend at least nine months in jail after he was sentenced for insider trading.

The Perth businessman showed little emotion as Justice Stephen Hall of the Supreme Court of Western Australia sentenced him to 18 months in jail, with a minimum of nine months. He was ordered to pay a $10,000 good behaviour bond and a $20,000 fine.

This month a jury found the 54-year-old father of two guilty of insider trading relating to information about LNG Limited's 2012 takeover bid for Westside Corporation.

The corporate regulator, Australian Securities and Investments Commission, alleged Noske bought 750,000 shares in Brisbane gas producer WestSide Corporation in February 2012 after being consulted by the managing director of LNG Limited on how WestSide's joint venture partner Mitsui might react to the bid.

Noske was an asset manager for Mitsui in Australia until mid-2011.

His defence argued he had no knowledge of the bid when he bought the shares based on his own analysis of the stock but Justice Hall said he found this "implausible" given evidence on Noske's communications with LNGL boss Maurice Brand and a contact Noske had maintained at Mitsui.

The price of WestSide shares increased by almost 60 per cent following its announcement days later it had received a takeover bid.

Justice Hall said he was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt Noske knew the information he possessed was material and not publicly available and it was the information that motived Noske to purchase the shares.

He said the gross profit of $51,246 did not reflect Noske's intentions but the more than $222,000 he invested demonstrated he was serious and confident in the information he had. He said Noske had not appeared "contrite" during the trial.

"The value of the information was high and clearly apparent," Justice Hall said.

Mr Noske's wife cried in the public gallery as Justice Hall declared the circumstances "too serious" for the sentence to be suspended.
